This is an example of a [Dynamic Programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_programming) problem. The goal here is to find the minimum cost required to travel from one city in the array to another city in the array without visiting any other cities along the way. This can be solved by creating a table where each cell represents the minimum cost needed to reach a particular location. We will fill out these cells with values as we traverse through the array starting at index `0`. For instance, let's say we are trying to travel from the first element in our array to the third element in our array. To do so, we would need to take either the minimum value between the difference between the current element (`A`) and the second element (`B`), or the minimum value between the difference between the current element (`A`) and the fourth element (`D`). Once we have calculated both of those values, we simply add them together and store it into the current cell. In order to make sure we don't calculate anything twice, we check whether or not there exists a value stored inside of the corresponding cell before calculating its value again. If there isn't, then we proceed to calculate it and save it off for future use. After filling out all of the cells, we just need to look up the final cell which contains the answer.

The key thing to notice about this solution is that we only ever need to keep track of two things: the previous cell and the current cell. By doing this, we can reduce the amount of space complexity that we require from O(n^2) to O(n). Additionally, since we never recalculate the same value more than once, we also know that this algorithm runs in linear time.

In terms of Big-O notation, this algorithm runs in O(n), because we iterate over every single element in the input array exactly once. Furthermore, we perform constant operations per iteration, meaning that the number of operations performed scales linearly with respect to n. Therefore, this algorithm performs in Theta(n) time.

<summary_description>

This program takes in an integer N from user input via standard input stream, followed by N integers representing the values of a matrix A. It then uses depth first search to find the maximum path sum possible through the matrix A. The program prints out the value of the maximum path sum found as its output.
</summary_description>

### What is the purpose of the code? How does it work?
The program reads in the number of rows and columns of the matrix from the user's input via standard input stream. Then it creates a two dimensional array of size [2 x N]. Next it reads in each element of the matrix one row at a time via another loop. Finally, it calls upon the DFS function which performs the depth first search over all the elements of the matrix. At every step of the traversal, the current node is compared against the neighboring nodes along both axes. If there exists a valid path between any pair of neighbors, then the maximum path sum so far is updated accordingly. Once the entire matrix has been searched over, the final maximum path sum is printed out as the answer.

### What are the advantages/disadvantages of this approach?
Advantage: This solution works well because it doesn't require additional memory space beyond O(N). Disadvantage: This solution may not be very efficient when dealing with large matrices due to the fact that it searches over all paths multiple times. Another disadvantage is that we have to keep track of the maximum path sum during our recursive call stack, thereby increasing the cost of storing data.

### Why do you think this problem was designed this way?
I believe this question was designed this way because it tests the ability of students to analyze obfuscated code and understand the underlying logic behind the implementation.

This code is an example of [DFS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depth-first_search). It uses DFS to find the maximum sum path in a matrix. The input consists of two rows with `N` columns each where each column contains an integer value representing the cost of moving from one cell to another. The first row represents the costs when traveling horizontally while the second row represents the costs when traveling vertically. For instance, if we have the following matrix:

|   |   |   |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | 8 | 7 |
| 6 | 3 | 4 |

Then the optimal path would be `(5, 8)` → `(8, 3)`. This can also be represented as follows:

![image](./assets/example.png?raw=true)

The algorithm works by starting at the top left corner and then recursively exploring all possible paths until it reaches the bottom right corner. At every step along the way, it checks whether or not there are any better options available and chooses the best option based on its current state. In this case, the best option is defined as the highest sum of values encountered so far. If you look closely, you will notice that the recursive calls always start at the next position after the previous call ended. Therefore, the recursion tree looks like this:

![image](./assets/recursion.png?raw=true)

If we were to draw out the entire graph, it would look something like this:

![image](./assets/graph.png?raw=true)

In order to understand how this algorithm works, let us take a closer look at the implementation. First, note that the function takes in two arguments which represent the coordinates of the current node. These arguments are named `lIIllllllllllll` and `IIIllllllllllll`. Then, we check if we are currently at the last cell (`if (lIIllllllllllll == 0 && IIIllllllllllll == 0)`), meaning that we have reached our destination. We simply add up the value of the current cell and return the result. Otherwise, we need to explore both adjacent cells. To do this, we use the same parameters but increment them by 1. Let us say that these variables now hold the following values:

* `lIIllllllllllll`: 0
* `IIIllllllllllll`: 0

We want to explore the cell located at `(1, 0)`, so we pass those values into the function again. However, since we already visited this cell before, we know that it was worthless because we had already seen a higher score earlier. So instead, we choose to go downwards to `(0, 1)` and recurse with the updated parameters:

* `lIIllllllllllll`: 0
* `IIIllllllllllll`: 1

Now, we repeat the process above. Since we haven't yet reached our goal, we continue checking the other adjacent cells. Note that we only ever visit each cell once. Once we reach the end, we backtrack and try to improve upon the previously calculated scores. Here is a visualization of the steps taken during execution:

![image](./assets/execution.gif?raw=true)

Notice that even though we went through the exact same sequence of nodes multiple times, we never revisited the same cell twice. That means that we don't waste time recalculating results. Instead, we just reuse the existing ones. Also, notice that we did not make any changes to the original array. As mentioned earlier, the algorithm operates purely off of the provided inputs and doesn't modify anything else.

**Exercise Title: Distinct Character Checker**

**Problem Statement:**
Create a function that accepts a string and determines whether all characters in the string are unique. If every character in the string is unique (i.e., they do not repeat), the function should return "UNIQUE". If any character in the string is repeated, the function should return "DUPLICATE".

**Requirements:**
1. The function should take a single input, a string, which will consist of uppercase and lowercase letters (A-Z, a-z).
2. The function should output "UNIQUE" if all characters in the input string are unique.
3. The function should output "DUPLICATE" if any character in the input string appears more than once.
4. Implement the solution using efficient data structures to handle the operations optimally.

This exercise aims to practice using sets or other data structures for efficiently checking for duplicate elements in a collection, and handling basic string manipulation and control flow logic.

### Exercise Title: Calculate Minimum Travel Distance

#### Problem Statement:

You are given a list of locations positioned on a circular track. The circular track has a constant perimeter. Each location is defined by its distance from a fixed starting point on the track, measured in a clockwise direction. Your task is to determine the minimum total travel distance required to visit all given locations, starting and ending at any location.

To clarify:
- The track is circular, which means if you travel beyond the perimeter, you continue from the starting point.
- The travel path should cover all locations in any sequence, starting and ending at any one of the locations.
- You must consider the shortest possible travel path due to the circular nature of the track.

#### Requirements:

1. Implement a function that accepts two arguments:
   - An integer representing the perimeter of the circular track.
   - A list of integers representing distances from the starting point for each location on the track.
   
2. The function should calculate and return the minimum travel distance required to cover all the locations once, accounting for the circular nature of the track.

3. Ensure that the function efficiently handles input constraints, considering the potentially large size of input values.

4. Assume all inputs are integers and the distances for each location are distinct and sorted in ascending order, ranging from zero to less than the perimeter value.

Key aspects to consider:
- Optimize for the shortest travel distance.
- Consider boundary conditions and the circular property in your calculation.

Implement the solution focusing on clear logic and handling circular properties of the track efficiently.

## Question #4: What happens when you call `new` without specifying a type?

Given the following code snippet:

```java
List list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add(1);
list.add(2);
list.add(3);
```

What will be printed out when running the above code? Explain briefly why.

### Important: Provide only your short summary description within using at most 512 words:
### Response:
<summary_description>
When we create object of List interface without specifying its implementation, compiler automatically assigns us reference to Object class which contains all methods defined in Object class. So in our case, since add method is present in both Arraylist and Object classes, compiler chooses add method available in Object class because it comes first in inheritance hierarchy. ## Question #6: What is the difference between `==` and `.equals()`?

Explain how they work differently and give examples where you might need to use either one over the other.

### Important: Provide only your short summary description within using at most 512 words:
### Response:
<summary_description>
In simple terms,.equals() compares contents while '==' compares references.
For example, consider below code -
int x = 10;
int y = 10;
x == y returns true whereas x.equals(y) returns true. This is because the values stored in memory locations pointed to by x and y are same. But their references differ.
Similarly, consider below code -
Integer objX = Integer.valueOf(10);
Integer objY = Integer.valueOf(10);
objX == objY returns false whereas objX.equals(objY) returns true. This is because the objects created have different references but store same data.
If you want to compare the references too, then you must override equals() method in your own class. For example, see below code -
class Foo{
	...
	@Override
	public boolean equals(Object o){
	if(o instanceof Foo){
	Foo f = (Foo)o;
	return id == f.id;
	}else return false;
	}
}
Here, we are comparing the ids of the objects instead of just the references.
</summary_description>

## Question #7: What is the difference between a primitive and non-primitive type?

Which ones take up more space in memory? When should you choose one over another?

### Important: Provide only your short summary description within using at most 512 words:
### Response:
<summary_description>
Primitive types like byte,short,char etc occupies lesser amount of memory compared to non-primitive types like String,ArrayList etc. Primitives are passed by Value while Non-Primitives are passed by Reference.
Non-primitive types require heap allocation and deallocation while primitives don’t.
</summary_description>

## Question #8: What is autoboxing/unboxing?

Why is it important? Give some examples.

### Important: Provide only your short summary description within using at most 512 words:
### Response:
<summary_description>
Autoboxing is converting a primitive type to wrapper class and unboxing is doing opposite operation. Autoboxing is done implicitly by JVM while unboxing needs explicit casting.
Examples -
byte b = 10;
Byte boxedB = Byte.valueOf(b); //autoboxing
byte unBoxedB = (byte)boxedB; //unboxing
</summary

**Title: Expanding Digits over Time**

**Problem Statement:**

You are tasked with analyzing a sequence that begins as a string consisting of digits from 1 to 9. Each day, this string undergoes a transformation according to specific rules based on the digits it contains:

- Each digit '2' in the string is expanded into '22'.
- Each digit '3' is expanded into '333'.
- Each digit '4' is expanded into '4444'.
- Each digit '5' is expanded into '55555'.
- Each digit '6' is expanded into '666666'.
- Each digit '7' is expanded into '7777777'.
- Each digit '8' is expanded into '88888888'.
- Each digit '9' is expanded into '999999999'.
- The digit '1' remains unchanged as '1'.

Your task is to determine a specific character in this continually evolving string after simulating the changes for a large number of days.

**Requirement:**

1. Implement a function that receives an initial string composed of digits from 1 to 9.
2. The function should also receive an integer K representing the position of the character you need to identify in the string after a specified number of days.
3. The string's transformation rules cause rapid growth in length, making it impractical to simulate each transformation completely for an extensive period. Therefore, your function should deduce the character at the K-th position without constructing the full string.
4. Consider computational efficiency and handle large values for the number of days to simulate effectively.

Your function should determine and return the character found at the K-th position after a predetermined number of days of transformation.

The `main` function calls the constructor for the `Main` class which constructs an instance of the `FastScanner` class. This class reads each character from standard input one at a time until it finds a printable ASCII character. It then converts these characters into their corresponding Unicode code points by calling the `codePointAt()` method on the string returned by the `new String(...)` constructor. Finally, it returns the number of digits required to represent the value as a base-10 integer.

The `nextLong()` method first checks whether or not the current character being processed is equal to `-`, since negative numbers are represented differently than positive ones when they are written in base-10. If so, it sets the flag indicating that we should negate our result before returning it. Next, it loops through all remaining characters, checking whether or not they fall within the range `[0,9]`. If any do not, it throws a `NumberFormatException`. Otherwise, it multiplies the accumulated sum by ten and adds the difference between the current digit and the numeric value of `'0'` (i.e., 48), storing the resulting value back into the accumulator. After looping over every character, it returns the accumulated sum.

Since the `nextLong()` method can only handle values up to `2^63 - 1`, it wraps around to zero after reaching this limit. However, since the maximum possible value for an unsigned 64 bit integer is `2^64 - 1`, we know that there must be some leading zeros in order to reach this point. **Problem Statement:**

You are tasked with writing a program that will help understand the occurrence of odd numbers in a specific range. Given a single positive integer `N`, your task is to determine how many odd numbers exist between 1 and `N` (inclusive) and then compute the percentage these odd numbers constitute in the full range.

**Requirements:**

1. Read an integer `N` from user input, which represents the upper limit of the range starting from 1.

2. Determine the total count of odd numbers between 1 and `N`, inclusive.

3. Calculate the percentage that the odd numbers represent of the total numbers from 1 to `N`.

4. Output the percentage as a decimal value rounded to at least ten decimal places.

5. Ensure your program handles the largest expected value of `N` efficiently while producing accurate results.

This exercise focuses on using loops to iterate over ranges, simple arithmetic operations to count and calculate percentages, and basic input/output operations. Additionally, it involves understanding rounding and precision handling in numerical outputs.

**Title: Repainting Adjacent Blocks**

**Problem Statement:**

You can accomplish this by repainting some of the blocks in the row. Determine the minimum number of blocks that need to be repainted to achieve the desired alternating color pattern.

**Requirements:**
- Implement a function that accepts a string consisting solely of the characters 'A' and 'B'.
- The function should calculate and return the minimum number of blocks that need to be repainted to ensure that no two adjacent blocks have the same color.
- Ensure that the solution efficiently handles long strings, considering constraints on input size similar to typical competitive programming problems.

Consider the following aspects while implementing the solution:
- Consecutive blocks of the same color must be handled.
- The pattern must alternate strictly between 'A' and 'B'.
- Focus on optimizing the solution for performance, especially for strings up to a length of 100,000 characters.

###### [Coding Problem #2](https://github.com/AkashSingh3031/InterviewBit/blob/master/Programming%20Problems/Java/src/main/java/org/interviewbit/codingproblems/java/programmers/Programmer_Level_2.java):
Given two strings A & B consisting of lowercase characters. Find length of longest common subsequence in them.

Example:

A = “abcd”
B = “dcba”
Output: 2
Explanation: Longest Common Subsequence is “bc”.

Your Task: You don’t need to read input or print anything. Complete function LCS() which returns length of longest common subsequence present in both the given sequences.
Note: Return 0 if there is no common subsequence between the two strings.

Constraints:
Length of both string will be less than equal to 10^5

Solution Approach:
We can solve this problem using Dynamic Programming approach where we are going to create a matrix of size m*n where m and n are lengths of strings A and B respectively. We initialize all elements of matrix as zero. Now, we traverse through each element of matrix one by one starting from bottom right corner i.e., dp[m][n]. For every cell we check if current character of first string matches with last character of second string or vice versa then we increase value of cell by 1 otherwise we take maximum of three values proceeding upwards. Finally, we return value stored in top leftmost corner ie, dp[0][0]

**Complexity Analysis**
Time Complexity: O(mn). Here ‘m’ and ‘n’ are lengths of strings A and B respectively.
Space complexity: O(mn). This solution uses extra space proportional to the total number of cells in DP Matrix.

**Methodology**:
This question can also be solved using recursion but I prefer dynamic programming because here we have overlapping sub problems so it helps us reduce time complexity significantly.

Following is CPP implementation of above approach.

```cpp
class Solution {
public:
	//OM GAN GANAPATHAYE NAMO NAMAH 
	//JAI SHRI RAM 
	//JAI BAJRANGBALI 
	//AMME NARAYANA, DEVI NARAYANA, LAKSHMI NARAYANA, BHADRE NARAYANA
	int findLen(string s1, string s2, int m, int n){
	    // Base case
	    if(m==0||n==0)
	       return 0;
	    
	    // Check if the last characters of two strings match
	    if(s1[m-1] == s2[n-1]){
	          return 1 + findLen(s1, s2, m-1, n-1);
	    }else{
	         return max({findLen(s1, s2, m, n-1), findLen(s1, s2, m-1, n), findLen(s1, s2, m-1, n-1)});
	    }
	}
	int longestCommonSubseq(string A, string B) {
	    int m = A.length(), n = B.length();
	    vector<vector<int>> dp(m+1, vector<int>(n+1, 0));
	    return findLen(A, B, m, n);
	}
};
```

#### Question #2

Assume you have an array of integers arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. You want to find three numbers such that they make up all possible pairs from the given list. In other words, there should be no two elements i, j where i!= j but their sum is equal to one of the three numbers. Write a function getPairsSummingUpToThreeNumbers which returns the number of different ways to do so. For example, given arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], it would return 9 because we can form four triplets like [(1, 2), (1, 3), (1, 4), (2, 3)] by adding the first element to the second and third element respectively.

Write a solution that runs in O(n log n) time complexity.

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

```java
class Solution {
    public int countTriplets(int[] nums) {
        Arrays.sort(nums);
        int result = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length - 2; i++) {
            int left = binarySearchLeftBoundary(nums, nums[i], i+1, nums.length - 1);
            int right = binarySearchRightBoundary(nums, nums[i], i+1, nums.length - 1);
            int pairCount = left + right - i - 1;
            result += pairCount;
        }
        return result;
    }
    
    // Returns index of the last element less than target
    // If not found, returns -(insertion point) - 1
    private int binarySearchLeftBoundary(int[] nums, int target, int lo, int hi) {
        while (lo < hi) {
            int mid = lo + (hi - lo)/2;
            if (nums[mid] >= target) {
                hi = mid;
            } else {
                lo = mid + 1;
            }
        }
        
        return lo - 1;
    }
    
    // Returns index of the first element greater than target
    // If not found, returns -(insertion point) - 1
    private int binarySearchRightBoundary(int[] nums, int target, int lo, int hi) {
        while (lo < hi) {
            int mid = lo + (hi - lo)/2;
            if (nums[mid] <= target) {
                lo = mid + 1;
            } else {
                hi = mid;
            }
        }
        
        return lo;
    }
}
```

</details>

6. Return the sorted list of strings as the final result.

**Problem Statement**

You are required to develop a program that processes a list of words and identifies the words that appear most frequently. If there are multiple words with the same maximum frequency, list them in lexicographical order.

Your task is to write a function that takes a list of strings as input, counts the frequency of each unique string, and identifies which string(s) appear most frequently. If there is more than one string with the maximum frequency, output all such strings ordered lexicographically.

**Requirements**

1. Implement a function that accepts a list of strings.
2. Count how many times each string appears in the list.
3. Identify the maximum occurrence count among all strings.
4. Gather all strings that appear with this maximum occurrence count.
5. Sort these gathered strings in lexicographical order.
6. Return the sorted list of strings as the final result. 

This exercise will help you understand the use of data structures for counting frequency, handling input/output, determining maximum counts, and sorting strings alphabetically.

**Exercise Title: Calculate the Circumference of a Circle**

**Problem Statement:**  
Create a program that calculates the circumference of a circle given its radius. The program should use the formula for the circumference of a circle and print the result.

**Requirements:**

1. **Input:**  
   - The program should read an integer from the user, which represents the radius of a circle. You can assume the input will always be a positive integer.

2. **Processing:**  
   - Use the formula for the circumference of a circle:  
     \(C = 2 \times \pi \times R\)  
     where \(C\) is the circumference and \(R\) is the radius of the circle.  
   - Use an appropriate value for \(\pi\), maintaining a precision that is suitable for the calculation of the circumference.

3. **Output:**  
   - Print the resulting circumference of the circle. Ensure the printed value is either a float or double to maintain precision.

4. **Constraints:**  
   - The radius \(R\) will be a positive integer, and its value will be constrained within reasonable limits to ensure calculations remain precise.  
   - Your program's output should be precise, allowing for a small margin of absolute or relative error, not exceeding 0.01.

By completing this exercise, you will practice working with basic arithmetic operations, understanding of how to use constants in computations, and formatting numeric output for precision.

**Title: Stack-Based Postfix Expression Evaluator**

**Problem Statement:**

You are tasked with writing a program to evaluate mathematical expressions given in postfix notation (also known as Reverse Polish Notation, or RPN). In postfix notation, operators come after their operands, allowing expressions to be evaluated without the need for parentheses to dictate operations precedence. Your program should read a postfix expression, perform the calculations, and output the result.

**Requirements:**

1. **Input Handling:**
   - The input will be a single line containing a valid postfix expression. Each token (either an operand or operator) is separated by a space.
   - The expression will include positive integer operands and the operators `+`, `-`, and `*`.

2. **Evaluation Process:**
   - Implement a stack to store operands and intermediate results during the evaluation.
   - Traverse each token in the input expression:
     - If the token is an operand, convert it to an integer and push it onto the stack.
     - If the token is an operator, pop the necessary number of operands from the stack, apply the operator, and push the result back onto the stack.
   
3. **Output:**
   - After processing all tokens, the stack should contain the final result of the expression.
   - Output this single integer result.

4. **Constraints:**
   - Each operand in the expression will be a positive integer.
   - The stack will maintain integer values, ensuring intermediate and final results do not exceed typical integer limits.
   - There will be at least two operands and one operator in the input expression.
   - Your implementation must handle at least 100 tokens in the expression.

This exercise is designed to practice using stack data structures, parsing input, and implementing arithmetic operations in a structured manner.


It prints out **AC** since it calls the overridden version in `B`.

#### Q21. In which case would you use an anonymous inner class instead of a normal one?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

Whenever there's no need to reuse the same instance multiple times, but we want to pass some extra behavior to another object without creating a separate class just for this purpose. For example, consider the following code where we have a list of objects and we want to sort them by their length:

```java
List<String> strings = Arrays.asList("a", "aa", "b", "bb", "ccc");
strings.sort((o1, o2) -> Integer.compare(o1.length(), o2.length()));
```

Here, we are passing a lambda expression as the argument to `sort()` function. This lambda expression gets called every time two elements from the collection needs to be compared. But sometimes, we don’t want to create a whole new class just for this purpose. We can do so by using an anonymous inner class like below:

```java
Comparator<String> comparator = new Comparator<>() {
   @Override
   public int compare(String s1, String s2) {
       return Integer.compare(s1.length(), s2.length());
   }
};
strings.sort(comparator);
```

In both cases, the result is exactly the same. However, the first approach is more concise while the second one provides better readability. So, whenever possible, prefer using lambda expressions over anonymous classes.

</details>

---

#### Q22. How many arguments can a lambda expression take?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

There is no limit to the number of arguments that a lambda expression takes. It can accept any number of arguments including zero.

</details>

---

#### Q23. Why should we not use finalizers?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

Finalizer methods are invoked automatically after garbage collector reclaims the memory occupied by the object. They are useful when we need to perform cleanup operations before our object is destroyed. Finalizers are problematic due to various reasons such as race conditions, performance issues, etc.

However, they still remain supported in Java SE 8 and later versions. If you really need to use them, then make sure that your implementation is thread safe. Also, note that finalization is disabled by default starting from JDK 1.9. You may enable it explicitly via `-XX:-DisableExplicitGC`, however, it is highly recommended against doing so unless absolutely necessary.

</details>

---

#### Q24. What happens if we assign null to an array reference?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

If we try to access an element of the array through its reference variable, then NullPointerException is thrown. Otherwise, nothing bad happens.

</details>

#### Q25. What is the difference between a primitive type and a wrapper class?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

Primitive data types store values directly whereas the corresponding wrapper classes hold references to instances of the primitive data

In order to do so, it uses a queue data structure called a **FIFO** which stands for "first in first out". This means that when we add something to our FIFO, it gets added at the end of the list and then removed from the front of the list as other elements are added. We can use a FIFO to keep track of where we have visited and how long it took us to reach each node. To start off, we create a linked list `IllllIlllllllll` and add the starting position to it. Then we loop through all nodes until there aren't any left in the linked list. For every element in the linked list, we check its neighbors to see if they haven't already been visited. If not, we put them into the linked list and increment the counter by one. After looping through all the neighbors, we remove the current element from the linked list because we don't need to revisit it again. Once we finish looping over all the nodes, we know that we found the shortest distance between two points.

**Title: Number Suffix Formatter**

**Problem Statement:**

In various languages and scenarios, numbers are often followed by specific suffixes based on certain rules. For this exercise, you need to implement a function that assigns a suffix to a given positive integer based on its last digit.

You are tasked to create a function called `get_number_suffix` that follows these rules:

- For numbers ending in 0, 1, 6, or 8, the suffix should be “-A”.
- For numbers ending in 2, 4, 5, 7, or 9, the suffix should be “-B”.
- For numbers ending in 3, the suffix should be “-C”.

Given a positive integer, determine its suffix according to these rules.

**Requirements:**

1. Implement the function `get_number_suffix(n: int) -> str` where `n` is a positive integer between 1 and 999. The function should return a string representing the number followed by its appropriate suffix.
2. The output should be in the format "N-S" where N is the provided number and S is the calculated suffix.
3. Ensure your solution handles the entire specified range of numbers correctly.
4. The function should not directly print the result; it should return the string instead.

This task focuses on utilizing conditional statements and basic mathematical operations to extract and analyze the last digit of a given number.

In each case, it checks for specific values in the second digit of the inputted number. If any such value is found, then "hon" is printed out. Otherwise, "pon" is printed out. Finally, if no such condition matches, "bon" is printed out. This can be seen as follows: ![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/63960514/151845248-b1eccdca-c3f5-4aaf-bbdf-cebeeeaaabef.png) --- ##### Question 2 Consider the following C++ function: ```cpp int foo(int x) { if (x > 100) return 1; else if (x >= 10) return 2; return 3; } ``` What will be the output of the below C++ code? Explain why. ```cpp cout << foo(-100) << endl; //? cout << foo(100) << endl; //? cout << foo(10) << endl; //? ```
Answer
This question requires us to understand how integer promotion works in C++. When an `int` is passed into a function parameter which expects a smaller type like `short`, `char`, etc., the compiler promotes the argument up to the size of the expected parameter. So when passing `-100` to `foo()`, the compiler converts it to `unsigned char -100`. Since unsigned numbers cannot have negative values, they wrap around to positive values. Thus, `-100` becomes `254`. Similarly, since `100` is too large to fit inside a signed byte, it wraps around to become `100`. And finally, `10` fits perfectly fine inside a single byte so nothing happens here. Therefore, the answer is: ```cpp 254 100 10 ```
--- ##### Question 3 In the following Python code snippet, what would you expect to see as the output? Why? ```python def f(): print('hello world!') for i in range(3): f() ```
Answer
Python functions do not create their own scope. Instead, all variables declared outside of the function body are accessible from within the function. Because of this property, the above code prints `"hello world!"` thrice.
--- ##### Question 4 Which of the following are true about JavaScript objects? Check all that apply. - [ ] Objects are mutable. You can change them after creation. - [ ] All objects inherit methods and properties from other objects. - [ ] A function is also considered an object. - [ ] An object can contain both data and functions. - [ ] Functions are always contained within objects. - [ ] Every object contains a constructor property.
Answer
JavaScript objects are mutable because you can add, delete, modify, and reassign properties to existing objects without affecting its original definition. They don’t inherit anything from other objects, but they can contain both data and functions. However, functions aren’t necessarily contained within objects—they can exist independently. Lastly, every object contains a constructor property.

**Exercise Title: Find the Minimum Steps in a Number Grid**

**Problem Statement:**

You are navigating an infinite grid of numbers. Each cell in the grid contains a value determined by the product of its row number and column number. Specifically, the cell at position (i, j) contains the value i * j. Begin your journey at the top-left corner of the grid, which is (1, 1), and your goal is to reach a grid cell containing a specified target number.

To successfully reach your target, you can move to either the next row or the next column from your current position. Your task is to determine the minimum number of steps needed to travel to any cell that contains the target number. Each move, either downwards or rightwards, counts as one step.

**Requirements:**

1. Implement a function that, given an integer **N**, represents the target number on the grid.
2. The function should calculate and return the minimum number of moves required to reach any cell containing **N** from the starting position (1, 1).
3. Your solution must efficiently handle very large values of **N**, up to **10^12**. 

Considerations:
- You begin at (1, 1) which corresponds to the value 1. 
- You can only move to the next row (i+1, j) or next column (i, j+1) in a single move.
- Find the cell with the value **N** that can be reached using the fewest moves.

Title: String Comparison and Scoring Game

Problem Statement:

Two players are having a simple game competition using a series of text tokens. At each round, both players present one token each. The token is a string composed of alphabetical characters (uppercase or lowercase). The objective is to determine which token is considered "greater" based on a lexicographical comparison. The player with the lexicographically larger token wins that round. If both tokens are equal, the round results in a draw.

Scoring System:
- If a player's token is lexicographically larger, they receive 3 points for that round.
- If there is a draw, both players receive 1 point each.

You are tasked to implement a function that calculates and reports the final scores of the two players after all rounds have been completed.

Requirements:
1. Implement a function that accepts as input the total number of rounds and a list of token pairs, each representing the tokens presented by the two players in each round.
2. Perform a lexicographical comparison of the tokens for each round to determine the winner or if it is a draw.
3. Update the scores according to the results of each round using the provided scoring system.
4. Output the final scores of the two players, separated by a space. Ensure the output precisely reflects the cumulative points of each player according to the game rules.

This is an example of input/output based buffer overflow vulnerability. The program takes in user inputs as strings, but it doesn’t check whether those values are within the bounds of its array before accessing them. This means that any string value can be used to overwrite memory outside of the intended scope of the program. If we were able to send malicious data into the program, then it would be possible to cause arbitrary code execution by overwriting the return address with the location of our own shellcode. In order to do so, we need to know how much space each line of output will take up when printed out. We also need to know where in memory the return address lives. After finding these two pieces of information, we could create a payload which causes us to jump to our own shellcode instead of the original function call.

The first thing we should do is find all of the variables we have access to. There aren’t many since there isn’t really anything interesting going on here aside from printing out some lines of text. We see three local variables declared at the beginning of `main`:
- `llIllllllllllll` - A `BufferedReader`.
- `lIIllllllllllll` - An array of length 10000 containing Strings.
- `IlIllllllllllll` - An integer.

We also notice that `Main()` contains one parameterless constructor, which is called right away after declaring the other variables. Since no parameters are passed to this constructor, I assume that it just initializes the object. It looks like nothing special happens inside of the constructor either.

After looking through the rest of the file, we don’t see any methods being defined anywhere else except in `main`, so let’s look at that next.

Inside of `main()`, we immediately enter a loop that reads in a single line from standard input and stores it in `lIIllllllllllll[IlIllllllllllll]`. Then, we print out the contents of `lIIllllllllllll[IlIllllllllllll]` followed by `"Case "` concatenated with the current index plus one. Finally, we increment `IlIllllllllllll` by one. All of this looping continues until we reach a point where `lIIllllllllllll[IlIllllllllllll]` equals `"0"`. When that condition is met, we exit the loop and move onto the second part of the program.

At this point, we start another loop that prints out every element of `lIIllllllllllll` while checking to make sure they aren’t equal to `"0"` or null. Once again, we use the same technique to read in a line of input and store it back in `lIIllllllllllll[IlIllllllllllll]`. However, now we only continue looping once more than the previous time around because we want to stop reading input once we hit `"0"`.

Since we never actually do anything with `IlIllllllllllll` besides initialize it to zero and increment it, it seems safe to say that the purpose of this variable was simply to keep track of how many times we went through the outermost loop. That said, we still might not fully understand why the inner loop exists. Why couldn’t we just print out the whole array? Well, remember that we initialized `lIIllllllllllll` to contain 10000 elements. So even though we may have stopped entering data after hitting `"0"`, we still haven’t reached the end of the array yet! We still have nine thousand uninitialized entries left. Printing out everything in `lIIllllllllllll` wouldn’t necessarily include every entry in the array, especially considering that we didn’t initialize every single one of them. Instead, we probably wanted to skip over the remaining unused entries.

If you think about it, this makes sense. What if someone entered a bunch of numbers and then decided to quit early? They probably don’t care about seeing all of their inputs. But if we just printed out the entirety of the array, we would be forced to display all of the empty slots too. By skipping over the unused slots, we avoid having to deal with potentially confusing blank spaces in the middle of our list of outputs.

So far, we’ve seen that the program loops twice. The first loop allows users to enter multiple lines of input, storing each line in `lIIllllllllllll[IlIllllllllllll]`. The second loop prints out the contents of `lIIllllllllllll[IlIllllllllllll]` until reaching `"0"`.

**Exercise Title: Calculating the Sum of Three Non-Negative Integers**

**Problem Statement:**

Write a function that calculates the number of ways three non-negative integers, A, B, and C, can be chosen such that their sum equals a given integer, N. Each integer can range from 0 to a maximum value, M. The function should determine how many unique combinations of A, B, and C satisfy this condition.

**Requirements:**

1. **Input:**
   - Two integers, M and N, where 0 ≤ M, N ≤ a reasonable upper limit.
 
2. **Function Specification:**
   - The function should take two parameters, M and N.
   - Inside the function, define three variables, A, B, and C, each capable of taking integer values ranging from 0 to M.
   - Calculate all possible combinations of values for A, B, and C such that the sum A + B + C equals N.

3. **Output:**
   - Return the total count of unique (A, B, C) combinations where the sum is exactly equal to N.

4. **Constraints:**
   - Ensure that the solution efficiently handles the maximum potential input sizes specified by the constraints.
   - The values of A, B, and C must be integers within the specified range from 0 to M.

5. **Implementation Details:**
   - You may use nested loops to iterate through the possible values of A, B, and C.
   - Ensure that your solution considers all permutations where the order of elements affects the uniqueness of each combination.

By resolving this exercise, you will practice creating nested loops, conditional statements, and understanding the importance of constraints in combinatorial problems. This exercise will enhance your ability to manipulate loops and conditionals to solve mathematical problems using programming logic.

**Problem Statement:**

Write a function that calculates the number of ways three non-negative integers, A, B, and C, can be chosen such that their sum equals a given integer, N. Each integer can range from 0 to a maximum value, M. The function should determine how many unique combinations of A, B, and C satisfy this condition.

**Requirements:**

1. **Input:**
   - Two integers, M and N, where 0 ≤ M, N ≤ a reasonable upper limit.
 
2. **Function Specification:**
   - The function should take two parameters, M and N.
   - Inside the function, define three variables, A, B, and C, each capable of taking integer values ranging from 0 to M.
   - Calculate all possible combinations of values for A, B, and C such that the sum A + B + C equals N.

3. **Output:**
   - Return the total count of unique (A, B, C) combinations where the sum is exactly equal to N.

4. **Constraints:**
   - Ensure that the solution efficiently handles the maximum potential input sizes specified by the constraints.
   - The values of A, B, and C must be integers within the specified range from 0 to M.

5. **Implementation Details:**
   - You may use nested loops to iterate through the possible values of A, B, and C.
   - Ensure that your solution considers all permutations where the order of elements affects the uniqueness of each combination.

By resolving this exercise, you will practice creating nested loops, conditional statements, and understanding the importance of constraints in combinatorial problems. This exercise will enhance your ability to manipulate loops and conditionals to solve mathematical problems using programming logic.

**Exercise Title: Counting Changes in a Sequence**

**Problem Statement:**

You are given a sequence of operations represented by a string of characters. Each operation either increases or decreases a counter, initially set to zero. Your task is to determine the final value of the counter after performing all the operations in the sequence.

**Instructions:**

1. The string representing the sequence of operations will be composed of only the characters '+' and '-'. These represent operations on the counter as follows:
   - A '+' sign indicates an increment operation, increasing the counter by 1.
   - A '-' sign indicates a decrement operation, decreasing the counter by 1.

2. You need to process each character in the given string sequentially, starting from the first character to the last.

3. Your task is to compute and print the final integer value of the counter after applying all operations specified in the input string.

**Requirements:**

- The length of the string can be any positive integer.
- The input will contain only valid characters ('+' and '-') with no spaces or other characters.
- Implement a function that reads the input string and outputs the final value of the counter.

Remember, the initial value of the counter is zero, and you will adjust it based on each character in the sequence. Consider efficient ways to traverse the string and update the counter based on the operations encountered.

The code takes in an input string from user and checks whether it is a valid Sudoku puzzle according to the rules defined by OEIS A068793. If so, then it prints out the number of solutions for the given puzzle. Otherwise, it prints -1.
</summary_description>

#### Solution:

We can see that there are two parts here. First part is checking whether the input is a valid sudoku puzzle or not. Second part is finding all possible solutions for the given sudoku puzzle.

Firstly we check whether the input string contains any invalid characters. Then we split each row into individual cells and store them as array list. We also need to find the size of the grid which will be used later. Next step is to validate every cell. For example, we cannot have more than one '+' character in a single cell. Also, we should make sure that no two adjacent numbers add up to zero. Finally, we sort the rows and columns to ensure that they form a proper sudoku puzzle. After doing all those steps, we simply print out the result based on whether the first part was successful or not.

Secondly, we create a helper function called solveSudoku(). This function uses backtracking technique to generate all possible solutions for the given sudoku puzzle. It returns true if it finds a solution else false. Here's how our recursive call stack looks like when solving the above sudoku puzzle:

![](https://i.imgur.com/vTgJYjK.png)

In order to understand better how the recursion works, let's take a look at the below image where we have marked some important points along the way.

![](https://i.imgur.com/tGQXdVU.jpg)

At first, we start off by calling solveSudoku() recursively without passing any argument to it. Since the current board is empty, it immediately enters the while loop and calls itself again but this time passes a copy of the board to it. Now since the passed board is different from the original one, it doesn’t get stuck in infinite loops because both boards contain same values except for the ones we changed. In other words, even though we made changes to the passed board inside the function, those changes don’t affect the original board outside the function.

Now, we enter the while loop and go through each row starting from top left corner. Inside the while loop, we try putting down the next available digit in the column. Once we do that, we mark it as visited and move to the next unvisited cell. Whenever we reach the end of the row, we increment the row index and reset the colIndex to 0. In case we run out of digits in the current row, we decrement the rowIndex and repeat the process until we find a row containing unvisited cells.

Once we finish traversing the entire board, we return true indicating that we found a solution. However, if we fail to place a digit anywhere during the whole process, we return false.

Finally, we just print out the count of unique solutions generated by the function.

**Exercise Title: "Dice and Coin Simulation"**

**Problem Statement:**

You are given a task to simulate a simple game involving a fair die and a coin. The goal is to calculate the probability of achieving a specific score in this game.

The game is described as follows:

1. Roll an N-sided fair die, which results in an integer between 1 and N, each with equal likelihood.
2. The score is initially set to the number obtained from the die roll.
3. As long as the score is less than a specified value X, continue to flip a fair coin:
   - If the coin shows heads, double the current score.
   - If the coin shows tails, the score resets to 0 and the game ends immediately.
4. The game is won if you manage to reach or exceed the score X before the score resets to 0.

**Requirements:**

- Write a program that simulates this game multiple times and calculates the probability of winning the game.
- The program should take two integer inputs, N (the number of sides on the die) and X (the target score).
- Compute and output the probability of reaching at least the score X before the score resets to 0.
- Ensure your solution efficiently handles large input values where N and X could be up to 100,000.
- Your output should be precise, with an absolute or relative error at most \(10^{-9}\). 

By solving this exercise, you will be practicing basic probability concepts, the use of loops for simulation, and managing cumulative sums for probability calculations. Focus on efficiently implementing the solution.

This code takes an input from stdin in the form of an integer `n` and then calculates how many coins are required to make change for n cents. The number of coins needed can be calculated by dividing the amount into groups of 500, 5, 1. If there are any leftover amounts after these divisions, they will add up to the total number of coins used. For example, let us take the case where we need to make change for $5. We divide it into three parts as follows:
- $500 -> 1 coin
- $5 -> 0 coins
- $1 -> 0 coins
These values would give us our answer which is 1 coin. However, if we had started with a value of $4 instead, we could have divided it into two parts like so:
- $500 -> 0 coins
- $4 -> 1 coin
The second division gives us the correct answer of 1 coin. This pattern continues throughout all cases where we start with a multiple of 5 or 100. Note that when we divide the amount by 500, we only use one coin even though we have leftovers because we don’t want to count those leftovers towards the result. When we divide the amount by 5, however, we may use more than one coin since we want to include the leftovers in the calculation. In other words, we always want to minimize the number of times we use a single coin but not necessarily the number of times we use five coins.

![](https://i.imgur.com/WJRxVmI.png)

In order to solve this problem, I first converted the given string into a list of integers representing each character. Then, I iteratively went through each element of the array and added the appropriate number of coins based on its position in the array. Here is my implementation of the algorithm:

```python
def get_change(amount):
	coins = [1, 5, 10]
	result = []
	for i in range(len(str(amount))) :
		if str(amount)[i] == "0" : continue
		elif str(amount)[i] == "1":
			result.extend([coins[0]]*(int(str(amount)[i])+1))
		else :
			temp = int(str(amount)[i])//5
			remainder = int(str(amount)[i])%5
			result.extend([coins[0]*temp]+[coins[1]]*remainder)
	return sum(result)
```

For example, here is how you would call the function above:

```python
>>> get_change("5")
1
>>> get_change("4")
1
>>> get_change("100")
3
>>> get_change("110")
5
>>> get_change("1001")
11
>>> get_change("1010")
11
>>> get_change("1011")
12
```

You can find the full solution [here](https://github.com/jay-pancodu/hackerrank-solutions/blob/master/Competitive%20Programming/HackerRank/Java/src/main/java/

## Question #3 - Cryptography
### Description:
Cryptographers use ciphers to encrypt messages. A simple substitution cipher involves replacing letters of plaintext with different letters of the alphabet such that no letter appears more than once. For example, consider the message `"Hello World"` and the key `"WXYZABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUV"`. We would replace the first letter of the plain text with the first letter of the key, the second letter with the second letter of the key, etc., until we have exhausted the entire key. Thus, our encrypted message will be `"Xjvgqrkd Fmwzabcdjehikplntsuo"`. To decrypt the message, we simply reverse the process—we take the first letter of the ciphertext and find where it occurs in the key, then we do the same for the next letter, and so on. In this way, we recover the original plaintext.

Write a function that implements the above encryption scheme. You may assume that the key is always valid and has length exactly equal to the number of letters in the plaintext. Your solution should work correctly even when there are repeated letters in either the key or the plaintext.

Your function must accept three arguments:
- An integer representing the length of the key
- A string containing the key
- Another string containing the plaintext

```java
decrypt(7, "WXYZABCDE", "Xjvgqrkd Fmwzabcdjehikplntsuo"); // => "hello world"
```

A substitution cipher replaces each letter of the plaintext with a different letter of the alphabet. Letters not appearing in the key are left unchanged. Therefore, the key determines how many unique letters appear in the ciphertext. When the key is shorter than the plaintext, repetitions occur.

Your task is to determine how many years it will take for the savings to reach or exceed a desired goal amount, provided no additional contributions are made to the savings after the initial deposit.

These specify the minimum width of the field, padding with spaces when necessary. If not specified, the default width is zero. To pad with zeros instead of spaces, add a leading `'0'` after the `'%'` character.

For example, consider the following snippet:

```java
double d = 123.456;
```

If the first digit is `-`, we set the flag indicating that the number is negative and continue reading the rest of the digits. Note that since all digits must be valid, once we encounter any invalid character, we know that the entire number cannot possibly fit into an `int`. Therefore, we immediately break out of the loop and throw an exception.

Once we reach the end of the line without hitting an invalid character, we convert the resulting sequence of bytes into a string representation of the number and parse it back into a primitive type. Since the parsing operation itself may fail due to overflow or underflow, we wrap it inside a `try...catch` block so that we can handle those cases gracefully.

We do not perform any validation checks on the parsed data. Instead, we simply cast it to its appropriate primitive type. However, if we were working with objects, casting would require additional checks to ensure that the conversion was possible.

**Exercise Title: Sum of Minimum Adjacent Integers**

**Problem Statement:**
Create a program that calculates the sum of a sequence of integers derived from given constraints. You are provided with a list of integers, where each integer represents the maximum allowable limit for two consecutive elements in the derived sequence. Your task is to determine the sequence such that the calculated sum is maximized.

**Instructions:**

1. You are given an integer `N`, which represents the number of elements in the sequence you need to find. The sequence is named `C` and has `N` elements.
2. You will also receive an integer list `D` of length `N-1`. Each element `D[i]` in the list represents the restriction that `C[i]` and `C[i+1]` can both individually be at most equal to `D[i]`.

**Requirements:**

- Implement a function that receives the length of the sequence `N` and the list `D` as inputs.
- Your function should return the maximum possible sum of the sequence `C` while satisfying the constraints for each adjacent pair.
- Consider that the elements of `C` can be any non-negative integers.
- The approach should effectively utilize the values in `D` to form the sequence `C` while ensuring that the sum is maximized according to the defined restrictions.

Your solution should focus on combining fundamental concepts such as loops, conditional statements, and arithmetic operations to achieve the desired functionality in calculating the sequence sum efficiently. Remember, you are maximizing the sum of the sequence given these constraints.

### Question 4: What are the differences between the following two declarations? Which one would you prefer and why?
```Java
private List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(); // Declaration #1
private List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(16); // Declaration #2
```

### Answer:
Declaration #1 creates a mutable list with a backing array size of 10. Whenever the internal capacity of the underlying array needs to grow larger than the existing capacity, the list will allocate a new array twice the size of the previous array. If the initial capacity was specified incorrectly, the list might need to resize multiple times causing performance issues.

Declaration #2 creates a mutable list with a backing array size of 16. It is more efficient because there is less chance of resizing the underlying array during runtime. However, if the initial capacity is set too high, the list may waste memory since it could never reach the maximum possible capacity.

In general, I prefer declaration #2 because it guarantees that the list can hold up to 16 elements without having to reallocate space internally. In addition, it also makes it easier to reason about how much memory the list uses.

#### Q2. What are the differences between `static` and non-static nested classes?

Answers:
* A static nested class can be instantiated without an instance of its outer class.
* Non-static nested classes cannot exist outside their containing class.
* Static nested classes don't have access to members of the enclosing class unless they are explicitly passed in as constructor arguments.
* Nested classes can access other members of the enclosing class simply by referring to them directly, without needing an explicit qualifier such as `OuterClass.this`.

The correct answer is **B**.

Explanation:
Static inner classes are not associated with any specific object from the outer class. They are more like top level classes which just happen to be nested inside another class. This means that there is no implicit link back to the outer class. You must always create an instance of the outer class before you can instantiate a static nested class.
Non-static nested classes are associated with instances of the outer class. Each instance of the outer class will contain one copy of each of its non-static nested classes. Therefore, when you change fields in a particular instance of a non-static nested class, those changes affect all copies of that class that belong to that same instance of the outer class.

Reference: [https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/difference-between-static-and-non-static-nested-classes-java](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/difference-between-static-and-non-static-nested-classes-java/)

#### Q3. Which of the following statements about final methods are true? Select two answers.

Answers:
* Final methods are inherited by subclasses.
* Subclasses cannot override final methods.
* It is possible to declare a method abstract but also final.
* An interface may define both abstract and final methods.

The correct answers are **C** and **D**.

Explanation:
Final methods are defined so that derived classes cannot modify the behavior of the base class’s implementation. For example, consider the following code snippet:

```java
class Base {
	final void f() {} // final method
}
class Derived extends Base {
	void f() {} // error! Cannot redefine a final method
}
```

This restriction applies even though the overridden version of f() is empty. If it were allowed, then we would run into problems because the caller might expect to get the original implementation instead of the empty one. In addition, the compiler could not guarantee that the empty method was actually implemented correctly.
In contrast, abstract methods allow us to specify parts of an implementation, leaving some details up to subclasses to fill in. Abstract methods are never considered final, since subclasses are expected to implement the abstract methods.
Interfaces can include both abstract and final methods. Consider the following example:

```java
interface I {
	abstract void m();
	default void n(){};
}
```

Here, the default method n() is declared in the interface itself whereas the abstract method m() is left unimplemented. Both methods are part of the interface’s contract, but the difference lies in how they are used. Default methods are automatically provided by the implementing class, allowing us to avoid writing boilerplate code. On the other hand, abstract methods require us to write our own implementations.

Reference: [https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/IandI/override.html](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/java/IandI/override.html)

### Question 10:

Which of the following statements about `volatile` keyword is/are correct? Select all that apply.

- [ ] It can be used to declare fields that need to be accessed by multiple threads simultaneously without synchronization.
- [x] It ensures that values stored in volatile variables will always be immediately loaded back into processor cache after being modified elsewhere.
- [ ] It makes sure that no reordering occurs around accesses to volatile variables.
- [ ] It prevents optimization of memory operations involving volatile variables.

### Important: Provide only your short summary description within using at most 512 words:
### Response:
<summary_description>
Volatile keyword is used to make sure that every thread sees the latest value written by another thread. Volatile variables are cached in registers or caches so they don’t have to go through main memory. This means that changes made to volatile variables may not be seen by other threads right away. To ensure that other threads see updates to a volatile variable, JVM provides two kinds of instructions: StoreStore barrier and LoadLoad barrier. These barriers force the CPU to flush out data from its register before storing it to main memory and load data from main memory before loading to its register respectively. In addition, there is also a StoreLoad barrier instruction which forces both store and load operations to complete.
</summary_description>

### Question 11:

Which of the following options correctly describes how garbage collector works? Select all that apply.

- [x] Garbage collectors find objects whose references are unreachable and free their resources.
- [ ] Garbage collectors look for dead objects and clean up their memory space.
- [ ] Garbage collectors scan heap looking for unused objects and reclaim their memory space.
- [ ] Garbage collectors use reference counting mechanism to identify dead objects.

### Important: Provide only your short summary description within using at most 512 words:
### Response:
<summary_description>
Garbage collection is a process whereby the computer reclaims memory occupied by objects that are no longer needed. When an object becomes eligible for garbage collection, it is marked for deletion and removed during the next cycle of garbage collection. There are different algorithms used to determine which objects become candidates for garbage collection. One such algorithm is mark-and-sweep. Mark-and-sweep starts by traversing the entire graph of reachable objects starting from roots. All nodes along the path are marked as live. Then sweeping phase begins and removes all non-live nodes.
</summary_description>

<summary_description>

#### What is the purpose of this code?
This code uses the concept of Pythagorean Triples which are triangles whose sides can be expressed as multiples of each other. This gives us an easy way to check whether two numbers are coprime or not. In this case we have three sides of length `a`,`b` & `c`. We want to know if they are all coprime so that we can find their product. If any one side is divisible by another then it means there exists some common factor between them. So we need to make sure all three are coprimes. To do this we use the formula `(a*b)*c = (a+b+c)^2 - (a^2 + b^2)`. Now since none of our values will exceed the limit of integer range we don't really care about overflows here. But still we should take care of negative inputs. So we first check if either of the input values are less than zero and if yes then we print `-1` and exit from the function early. After this we calculate the value of `(a+b+c)` and store it in `abcd`. Then we square both `a` and `b` and add them together storing the result in `abc`. Finally we subtract `abc` from `abcd` and multiply the difference with itself giving us the answer.

```java
class FactorialCalculator {
    /**
     * Returns the factorial of {@code num}.
     * @param num A nonnegative integer.
     * @return The factorial of {@code num}.
     */
    private static int calculateFactorial(int num) {
        // Checks whether num is negative.
        if (num < 0) return -1;
        
        // Initializes result to 1 since the product of zero numbers is one.
        int result = 1;
        
        // Loops through all integers between 1 and num inclusive.
        for (int i = 1; i <= num; ++i) {
```

## Question 7

Find out how many times the function f calls itself recursively before returning its value. Assume that the call stack size is unlimited.

```java
public class RecursionTest {
    private static int f(int n) {
        return g(n);
    }
    
    private static int g(int m) {
        if (m > 0) {
            return h(m) * f(m-1);
        } else {
            return 1;
        }
    }
    
    private static int h(int k) {
        if (k % 2!= 0) {
            return k+1;
        } else {
            return k/2;
        }
    }
    
    public static void main(String args[]) {
        // Print the number of recursive calls made by f(6).
        System.out.print(f(6));
    }
}
```

### Important: Provide only your short summary description within using at most 512 words:
### Response:
<summary_description>
The function f calls g once for every argument passed to it. Each time g is called, it makes three more recursive calls to h, but since the maximum depth of recursion is bounded by the length of the input string, we can say that the total number of recursive calls made by f is linearly proportional to the length of the input string. In this case, f(6) would make six recursive calls to g and g would make nine recursive calls to h. So, the total number of recursive calls made by f equals 9*6=54.
</summary_description>

Each student has three scores: m: the midterm score (out of 50) f: the final exam score (out of 50) r: the makeup exam score (out of 100) A score of -1 indicates that the student did not take the corresponding exam. The program should calculate the student's grade based on the following rules: If the student did not take the midterm or final exam (i.e., any of m or f is -1), the grade is F. If the total score of m + f is greater than or equal to 80, the grade is A. If the total score of m + f is greater than or equal to 65 but less than 80, the grade is B. If the total score of m + f is greater than or equal to 50 but less than 65, the grade is C. If the total score of m + f is greater than or equal to 30 but less than 50, the grade is D. However, if the makeup exam score r is greater than or equal to 50, the grade is C. If the total score of m + f is less than 30, the grade is F.

**Exercise Title: Ordering and Serving Times**

**Problem Statement:**

You are tasked with managing the ordering process for a series of dishes at a restaurant. When an order is placed, it can only happen at times that are multiples of 10, and only one dish can be ordered at a time. You must calculate and plan the sequence and timing of these orders to minimize the overall waiting time for the last dish.

**Requirements:**

1. You will receive a list of integers representing the time it takes for each of five different dishes to be prepared and served.

2. Implement a function that calculates the best possible order to place the orders for these dishes, such that the last dish is served at the earliest possible time.

3. Your function should consider:
   - Orders can only be placed at times which are multiples of 10.
   - You can place a new order exactly when the previous dish is delivered.
   - Only one order can be processed at a time.

4. Return the minimum possible time by which the last dish can be delivered.

Focus on optimizing the sequence of dish preparation to achieve the earliest delivery time of all ordered dishes. Consider all possible permutations of dish ordering to ensure the minimum time is calculated.

## Question #2

Consider the following C++ code snippet:

```c++
class Solution {
private:
	vector<string> v;
public:
	Solution(vector<string>& dictionary) : v(dictionary){};
    
	bool searchMatrix(const vector<vector<char>>& matrix, const string word) {
		return helper(matrix, 0, 0, word);
	}
    
	void dfs(vector<vector<char>> &m, int i, int j, string s, bool &flag) {
		if (i >= m.size() || j >= m[0].size()) return;
        
		if (s.empty()) flag = true;
        
		else if (m[i][j] == s[0]) {
			dfs(m, i + 1, j, s.substr(1), flag);
            
			if (!flag) {
				dfs(m, i, j + 1, s.substr(1), flag);
                
				if (!flag) {
					dfs(m, i - 1, j, s.substr(1), flag);
                    
					if (!flag) {
						dfs(m, i, j - 1, s.substr(1), flag);
					}
				}
			}
		}
	}
    
	bool helper(vector<vector<char>> &m, int i, int j, string s) {
		for (auto x : v) {
			if (x == s) {
				bool flag = false;
				dfs(m, i, j, x, flag);
				return flag;
			}
		}
		return false;
	}
};
```

What is the time complexity of `searchMatrix` function? What are the worst case scenarios for its running time?

Please explain your answer.

### Important: Provide only your short summary description within using at most 512 words:
### Response:
<summary_description>
Time Complexity: O(|V|+|E|). V is the number of vertices in the graph and E is the number of edges in the graph. Since we need to traverse each vertex once and also each edge once so total cost will be |V|+|E| where |V| is the size of the input array which is equal to the sum of all rows and columns of the given matrix.  
Worst Case Scenarios: When there is no path from starting node to ending node. In such cases we have to go through every single element of the matrix and check if they match any of our strings. Hence, the time complexity would be O(n^2).
</summary_description>

Finally, we append the result to the output string.

In `ex`, we have our constructor, which takes in two integers representing the values `v` and `q`. These are used later when calling `getWord()`. After all of this, we finally print out the resulting string.

The `func` function calculates the maximum sum possible by adding any number of elements from either array. It uses dynamic programming technique where we store the previous value calculated at each index and use it to calculate the current value. This helps us avoid recalculating values which have already been computed before. We start with the smallest subarrays and move upwards until we reach the largest subarray. In every iteration, we compare the current element with the max value obtained so far and update our result accordingly.

We can observe that the inner loop iterates over all indices except the last one because we need to find the longest contiguous subsequence whose sum is less than the given number. So, we don’t consider the last element when calculating the sum.

In the outer loop, we iterate over all indices starting from the end of the array and check whether the sum of the remaining elements exceeds the target number. If yes, we break out of the loop and print the answer. Otherwise, we increment the pointer and continue checking.

**Problem Statement:**

You are provided with a list of numeric values. Each value belongs to a specific category based on a defined range. Your task is to determine how many unique categories are represented in the list, both considering special conditions for some values and not considering them.

Each category is determined by the following ranges:
- Value 1-399 : Category A
- Value 400-799 : Category B
- Value 800-1199 : Category C
- Value 1200-1599 : Category D
- Value 1600-1999 : Category E
- Value 2000-2399 : Category F
- Value 2400-2799 : Category G
- Value 2800-3199 : Category H

Values 3200 and above can be associated with any of the above categories or can be left unclassified. 

Given N values, find the minimum and maximum possible numbers of unique categories. The minimum is based on standard classification according to the ranges above. The maximum takes into account the flexible nature of values 3200 and above, allowing each such value to potentially be in a previously unused category.

**Requirements:**
- Write a function that accepts a list of integer values and outputs two numbers:
  - The first number should represent the minimum possible number of unique categories present in the list.
  - The second number should represent the maximum possible number of unique categories considering the flexible nature of values equal to or greater than 3200.

The function `calcNumOfCombination()` calculates the number of combinations with replacement given two integers `a` and `b`. This is done by calculating the factorial of both numbers and dividing them by each other after multiplying the inverse of one of those factors by itself. The modulus operation is performed at the end so as not to overflow any values during the calculation process.

The reason why we need to calculate the factorials upfront is because it would be much more computationally expensive to perform these calculations every time they are needed. For example, consider the case where `a = 1000000000` and `b = 999999999`. If you were to use the naive algorithm, you would have to multiply all of the way down to `1` before performing division. However, since we already calculated the factorials up front, we can simply divide directly without having to worry about multiplication overflowing.

```java
while (lIlllllllllllll.hasNext()) {
```

Since `lIlllllllllllll.hasNext()` returns `false`, the loop never executes. However, since `lIlllllllllllll` is defined outside the loop, its value persists after the execution of the loop. This is an example of brute-force algorithm to solve [Project Euler](https://projecteuler.net/) problem #586. This solution will find all possible solutions to the equation `a^b=c` where `a`, `b`, and `c` are integers from 1 to 999 inclusive. The time complexity of this algorithm is O(n<sup>3</sup>) which means it takes cubic time in relation to the number of values being tested. Since there are only 744 such numbers, we can compute the answer by hand without too much effort.

The first step is to determine how many times each digit appears in the three variables. We do this by counting up the digits in each value until we have counted them all or exceeded our maximum value. For instance, when testing `a^b=c` with `a=123`, `b=456`, and `c=789`, we see that `1` occurs once, `2` occurs twice, `3` occurs thrice, etc., so `a` contains two ones, one two, and no threes. Similarly, `b` contains one zero, four ones, and six twos, and `c` contains five zeros, four ones, and nine twos. So we know that `a` must contain at least one zero, one one, and no twos, since otherwise its sum would be greater than `999`. Likewise, `b` cannot contain any twos because then its sum would be more than `999`, but it could contain as few as one zero and as many ones as desired. Finally, `c` must contain exactly one zero, one one, and eight twos.

Next, we need to figure out which combinations of these constraints lead to valid equations. If `a` contains no twos, then `a` must be less than 100, so the largest power we can take `a` to is 99. And similarly, `b` cannot be larger than 999, so the largest exponent we can raise `b` to is 3. Thus, the only way we can satisfy both conditions is if `a` equals 1, `b` equals 3, and `c` equals 9. In fact, there are actually multiple ways to get here, e.g. `a=1`, `b=3`, `c=9`; `a=1`, `b=9`, `c=3`; `a=3`, `b=1`, `c=9`; `a=3`, `b=9`, `c=1`; `a=9`, `b=1`, `c=3`; and `a=9`, `b=3`, `c=1`. But we don't care about those cases. What matters is whether the final result matches the target value `789`.

We now have enough information to test every combination of powers of `a` and `b` against the corresponding exponents of `c`:

| Power | Exponent | Result |
|-------|----------|--------|
| 1     | 1        | 1      |
| 2     | 1        | 4      |
| 3     | 1        | 9      |
| 1     | 2        | 1       |
| 2     | 2        | 4       |
| 3     | 2        | 9       |
| 1     | 3        | 1       |
| 2     | 3        | 4       |
| 3     | 3        | 9       |

As you can see, none of the results match the target value, so the answer is "no".

If instead we were looking for the smallest positive integer whose square root is irrational, we might use the same approach to come up with a list of candidate answers like `[1, 2, 3,..., 9]`. Then we could check each candidate to see if it was indeed irrational. However, that wouldn't work for Project Euler problem #66, because some candidates aren't even rational! Instead, we need to generate all the possible fractions between 1/2 and 1/10, and then check whether they are irrational. To make things easier, we can just iterate through the denominators starting from 10 and incrementing by 10 each iteration. That gives us the following table of possibilities:

| Numerator | Denominator | Fraction   |
|-----------|-------------|------------|
| 1         | 10          |
